To strive means to put in serious, sustained, and determined effort toward a goal — especially when it is difficult or takes a long time to achieve.

It is not just about trying something once. Strive suggests that you keep pushing, keep working hard, and don't give up easily. There is a sense of struggle and dedication built into the word.

She strives to be a better person every single day.

In that sentence, she is not just making a one-time effort. She is continuously working hard at it, day after day.

"Strive" carries a certain weight and seriousness. When you use it, you are saying that the effort is meaningful, persistent, and not easy. It suggests that the goal matters deeply to the person and that they are willing to face challenges to reach it.

Think of it this way: if "try" is turning a key in a lock once, "strive" is spending hours picking the lock, determined to open it no matter what.

Here is a simple scale to understand the intensity:

  • Try → a general, basic effort. Low pressure. "I'll try."
  • Strive → a serious, driven, ongoing effort against some difficulty. "I will keep working hard at this, no matter what."
  • Struggle → similar difficulty, but this word focuses more on how hard and painful the process is, rather than the goal.

So "strive" sits in the middle — it is more intense and serious than "try," but it focuses on your determined effort toward a goal rather than on your pain or suffering.

There are three main patterns:

1. Strive + to + verb (most common)
This is when you are working hard toward doing something.

He strives to improve his writing.
We must strive to treat everyone fairly.

2. Strive + for + noun
This is when you are working hard toward having or achieving something.

She strives for excellence in her work.
The team strives for perfection.

3. Strive + against + noun (less common)
This is when you are making a determined effort to fight or resist something.

They strived against injustice their whole lives.
He strives against his own bad habits.

Quick note on past tense: Both strove and strived are correct for the simple past. Strove is more traditional and is more commonly used in formal or literary writing. Striven is the traditional past participle (used with "have"), but strived is also widely accepted.

He strove to succeed despite every obstacle. ✅
He strived to succeed despite every obstacle. ✅
She has striven her whole life for this moment. ✅

Here are examples across different situations so you can see the full range of the word:

Personal growth:

She strives to become a little better every day.

Work and achievement:

The company strives for customer satisfaction above everything else.

Difficult circumstances:

Even with very little money, he strove to give his children a good education.

Values and ideals:

A good leader strives to be honest, even when honesty is uncomfortable.

Ongoing effort:

Scientists are striving to find a cure for the disease.

Fighting against something:

She strived against self-doubt her entire career and eventually became one of the best in her field.
The Tone of the Word — When Do People Use It?

"Strive" is slightly formal. You would hear it in:

  • Speeches and motivational writing ("We must strive for a better world.")
  • Mission statements from companies or organizations ("We strive to deliver quality.")
  • Literature and serious writing
  • Inspirational and philosophical contexts

In casual, everyday conversation, people tend to say "try hard" or "work hard" instead. But "strive" is perfectly natural in slightly serious or thoughtful conversation too.
The One Thing That Makes "Strive" Unique

Many words describe effort — try, attempt, endeavor, aim. What makes strive special is the combination of three things happening at once:

  1. Serious effort — not a half-hearted try
  2. Persistence — it keeps going over time
  3. Difficulty — there is something to push against

If any one of those three things is missing, "strive" starts to feel like the wrong word. A casual, easy, one-time effort is not striving. Striving is what you do when something matters to you, it isn't easy, and you keep going anyway.
